children.text: The news segment covered several major stories. A federal judge ruled the Clinton administration could not submit NAFTA to Congress for approval until its environmental impact was assessed, dealing a setback to supporters of the trade agreement. In California, a jury awarded $2.9 million to lettuce grower Bruce Church Inc. in a lawsuit against the United Farm Workers, who vowed to appeal rather than pay. A New York Times/CBS poll found that 53% of Latino/as surveyed supported reducing immigration levels, though a higher share than the general public said they would welcome immigrants in their neighborhoods. The Supreme Court issued a narrow five-to-four ruling suggesting that minority-drawn congressional districts with irregular boundaries could violate the rights of white voters. Latino legal organizations responded with immediate legal challenges, and Democratic Congressman Luis Gutierrez of Chicago, whose district could be affected, called for a fair and equitable process rather than a guaranteed outcome for any group.

Over a hundred Latino/a health and community organizations joined to announce the formation of the National Hispanic Latino AIDS Coalition, coordinating simultaneous press conferences in five cities. Maria Hinojosa spoke with Eunice Diaz, the only Latina member of the now-concluded National Commission on AIDS, who described the coalition as an unprecedented show of unity after years of fragmented efforts. Boston poet Marta Valentin offered a spoken-word commentary on the frustrations of underfunded Latino AIDS education agencies, noting that the bureaucratic competition for resources costs lives daily.

Following the Clinton administration's June 1993 bombing of Baghdad in retaliation for an assassination plot against former President George H.W. Bush, Latino USA gathered reactions from Latino/a residents in Miami and Los Angeles. Opinions were divided, with some expressing support for decisive action against Saddam Hussein and others questioning the military necessity and its potential to escalate international conflict.

Correspondent Mandalit del Barco reported on Sesame Street's new season-long focus on Latino/a culture, featuring performances by Los Lobos and Tito Puente, location shoots in Los Angeles and New York barrios, and the introduction of Rosita, a bilingual blue Muppet played by Mexican puppeteer Carmen Osbahr. Research showed Puerto Rican preschoolers had lower self-esteem than their white and African-American peers, prompting producers to address themes of identity, skin color, and cultural pride. Actors Sonia Manzano and Emilio Delgado, who have played Maria and Luis for over two decades, reflected on the significance of showing Latinos as everyday people on national television.

With Cuba signaling willingness to compensate U.S. companies for seized properties and retired military officers announcing a visit to the island, divisions within Miami's Cuban exile community were intensifying. Reporters Ivan Roman, Nancy San Martin, and Emilio San Pedro described fistfights outside radio stations between hardliners favoring a tighter embargo and recent arrivals who wanted to maintain contact with family still in Cuba. Analysts said the Clinton administration had not yet defined a clear Cuba policy, appearing to quietly accommodate both factions.

The episode closed with a personal commentary from John Guardo, a former New York City gang member, who described the impossible bind of trying to live a law-abiding life in a neighborhood where both gangs and police posed daily threats. Unable to trust law enforcement after repeated harassment, he wrestled with whether buying a gun for home protection was the only option left to him.
